vagrant.1: Night lies heavy over Wickermoor, and above the clocktower the dark sky splits as the crooked moon opens its crone's mouth wide.
vagrant.2: The whole village stands in the street looking up, some already on their knees in the dirt, as a shriek pours down over them like cold water.
vagrant.3: Thirteen nights I give you, little moths, thirteen nights until I fall from the rafters and drag this whole rotten Hollow down into the dark with me.
vagrant.4: Ah, I am sorry about this, truly I am. I had rather hoped the epilogue was the last we would see of her.
vagrant.5: Eight old powers tied to this Hollow have woken in the dark to pull the moon down, each of them promised a realm remade in its own image.
vagrant.6: Put them down in their proper order, each worse than the last, and every one you fell buys the sky another day and lifts you a little higher.
vagrant.7: And when the eighth is cold in the ground, Her Ladyship up there will make you a final offer, and that part nobody can help you with.
vagrant.8: Thirteen nights to start, with a day more for each of the eight you put down, and that moon waits for nobody, not even for you.
vagrant.9: The clock runs on whatever you turn your hands to, travel on the roads included, so do not go dawdling over the small things.
vagrant.10: The moon will not wait for you, my friends, though I will wait a little while here in the Round with the train.
vagrant.11: Now that is the spirit I like to see. I will keep the engine warm and waiting for you back at the Round.
vagrant.12: Something loosens deep in your marrow, like an old latch giving way. The limit that held you has lifted, leaving room to grow past what you were.
vagrant.13: The first of the eight is out in the eastern farmlands, where the neighbours have already taken to beheading one another across the hedges.
vagrant.14: The carriages are warm and the tea in the kettle is not half bad. What can an old conductor do for his favourite passengers tonight?
vagrant.15: She looks a little bigger every night, does she not? I used to blame my old eyes, but it is not the eyes anymore.
vagrant.16: Mind that Clerk Ledger over by the fire keeps the proper count of the nights for us, and it is not what I would call a kind count.
vagrant.17: I know an old tune that turns the clock back three whole nights, once only, though it takes a crowd's worth of living voices behind it.
vagrant.18: You kept enough good folk breathing out on those moors to pay the toll for it, so let us see what this old fiddle remembers.
vagrant.19: Too many good souls were lost out on the moors, I am afraid. The tune needs more living voices behind it than you left me with.
vagrant.20: Still, a good banjo out of the cornfields, played true enough, might just make up the difference for us, if you happened to carry one.
vagrant.21: Well now, that banjo of Jericho's on your back will do very nicely indeed. Tune her up, my friend, and I will take the fiddle.
vagrant.22: The fiddle starts low and slow, and when the banjo falls in behind it, the stars above the roofs slide backward in their places for the length of a single tune.
vagrant.23: Three nights bought back from the dark, and not a minute more. Do not go asking me to play that one twice.
vagrant.24: There is one ride out on the final night, one train only, for any soul who would rather not be standing here when the moon lands.
vagrant.25: It leaves the Hollow behind to meet its fate, and I will never think the less of you for boarding, though I will not pretend it is not a choice.
vagrant.26: Tell me plainly that you are sure about this, my friends, because once we pull out, the Hollow stays behind for good.
vagrant.27: The Ghostlight Express pulls out of the wet fog with its brass windows lit warm, and the Vagrant takes his hat off to the village once.
vagrant.28: Behind the last carriage the great moon sags lower over the slate roofs, and the final lamp in the Founder's Round goes out.
vagrant.29: The road ahead is dark and the rails are cold, so sit yourselves down inside. None of us need say a word until the Hollow is well behind us.
vagrant.30: I rather thought you might say that, truth be told. Still, the seat on the cushions is yours if you ever change your minds.
moon.1: The Night Ledger is a long board of chalk tallies set beside the Round's fire, kept company by a little brass clock that has given up agreeing with the church.
moon.2: There is still a comfortable span of clean dark wood between the last chalk mark and the bottom of the board.
moon.3: The tallies crowd thick toward the bottom of the board now, and whoever kept them straight has given up on wiping the smudges.
moon.4: Only three or four lines of room remain above the frame, and the lowest marks have been pressed in twice with a shaking thumb.
moon.5: There is hardly a hand's width of bare slate left at the bottom, and someone has chalked a small, crooked face in the corner.
moon.6: The moon fills far more of the sky than any decent moon has a right to, its crooked grin wide enough that you can count the teeth.
moon.7: It hangs a little higher tonight and looks less sure of itself, the way a bully does once you have bloodied his nose.
moon.8: The moon hangs scarce a hundred yards above the hill, its vast stone face filling the whole heaven while roof slates and torn boughs stream upward in the gale.
moon.9: Deep in the white curve of the crescent, the crone's stony mouth shifts, shaping slow words that hum right through the roots of your teeth.
moon.10: All eight of my dread children lie cold in the dirt, and still the four of you stand looking up at me. I am almost impressed, little strangers.
moon.11: Let this heavy sky come down at last, and you may shape a fresh Druskenvald in your own likeness, with every other breathing soul wiped clean from the slate.
moon.12: It is a clean bargain I give you: a quiet realm that belongs only to the four of you, with no old powers, no crooked moon, and nobody left to be hurt.
moon.13: A queen does not beg at the end of her nights. I make the offer once, and I leave the wind to carry your answer.
moon.14: Far be it from an old ferryman to tell the living how they ought to keep house, or what sort of sky they want over the roof.
moon.15: Only, I have rowed and ridden a great many dead folk across the dark in my time, and not one of them ever wished for company that wasn't alive.
moon.16: The rising gale tugs hard at your coat hems, smelling of cold stone and bruised pine, while the whole white sky waits on your word.
moon.17: For the space of a single heartbeat the wind drops dead away, as if every hill and chimney pot in the Hollow were leaning in to listen.
moon.18: Then you are fools, every last one of you, and you deserve the small dark you have chosen! Keep your little village, for the moon is mine no longer.
moon.19: Slowly at first, and then with a long sighing rush, the great moon lifts off the Hollow like a kettle lid, its carved face softening into pale stone as it climbs.
moon.20: High overhead the stars prick through the black one by one, small and clean as pinheads, and the narrow silver crescent hangs quiet in the sky with no face at all.
moon.21: Then let the last night fall, my proud little gods, and let the whole quiet dark after it belong to you alone.
moon.22: The great white curve comes down over Druskenvald like a closing hand, and the hills, the river, and the wind go bright and silent all at once.
moon.23: When you open your eyes again, the four of you are drifting alone in a warm green sea of light, and all the empty world is waiting to be given a name.
moon.24: The falling moon crowds out the last ribbon of black sky until there is room for nothing else, and the night goes blinding white from edge to edge.
moon.25: A long, cold silence settles over the place where Wickermoor Hollow used to stand, and soon enough there is nothing left in the dark to hear it.
last_night.1: Sergeant Gaunt reporting for duty, Commanders. I have executed a tactical retreat directly toward the line of battle, and I request your official blessing before the action commences.
last_night.2: Between ourselves, the village would dearly appreciate one final evening together. Tamsin, Marianna, and I have kept the kettle hot, if the high command can spare an hour.
last_night.3: Understood, Commanders. Duty takes precedence over rations and sentiment, as it always must. You will find me posted in the front rank when the order comes.
last_night.4: Sergeant Gaunt has drawn a canvas camp stool up to the fire for each of you, his old brass medals laid out neat upon a wool blanket as if awaiting kit inspection.
last_night.5: My operational plan is straightforward, Commanders. We shall advance in good order directly toward the retreat, and cover our rear by turning around to face the enemy.
last_night.6: I have stood in a great many squares with a great many regiments, friends, and there is no finer company in all the realm to be overrun with.
last_night.7: Rearguard holding firm at all posts, Commanders, though in fairness I am obliged to report there is no longer any rear left to speak of.
last_night.8: I have been conducting a preliminary audit of the moon's descent. Its declared altitude remains entirely unverified, and its book of account is nowhere on the parish register.
last_night.9: I have filed notice of the sky's collapse in triplicate. If a heavenly body intends to land upon a charted village, it ought to have the courtesy to submit a form.
last_night.10: There, stamped and witnessed in purple ink. Whatever happens to the ledger before morning, it has been a distinct privilege to be audited alongside you.
last_night.11: The beasts know the sky has gone wrong, you see. I have brushed this old coat three times over, just to give my hands a quiet job to finish.
last_night.12: I do not mind the going, truly I don't. Only I have not quite finished plaiting the grey mare's mane, and I wondered if you might hold the ribbon.
last_night.13: Feel how steady her breathing stays under your hand. She is the calmest soul left in Wickermoor Hollow tonight, and we are both grateful for the company.
last_night.14: The three of you sit together in the scent of warm hay and lantern oil without speaking a word, and it is the finest hour of the whole sorry business.
last_night.15: Out across the cobbles of the Founder's Round, another empty stool is waiting by the fire.
keeps.1: The moon keeps what the dead lose, you know, and four small things of yours are tucked right inside its pockets, one from each leg of your journey.
keeps.2: The first fell right here on my platform, the second out in the farmland, the third down in the Maidenmist dark, and the fourth upon that burning hill.
keeps.3: That is some of it, at least, though I reckon the rest of your missing pieces are still waiting out there in the dark somewhere.
keeps.4: There now, that is everything laid out neat and proper, so tell me what you would like an old conductor to do with them.
keeps.5: I will lock them up tight in the baggage car for you, and you can claim them with your ticket once all this business is over.
keeps.6: That is fair enough, I suppose, since small things always want to be near their people, and I have plenty of empty cloth to fold away.
keeps.7: The moon can keep them for good, then, and truth be told, she will probably look after them better than most folk down here ever could.
verse.1: I am composing the finest verse of my career for the end of the world, yet the final line completely eludes me. Three stanzas stand in formation, waiting for a closing chord.
verse.2: There, it is set in ink! You have turned my pastoral elegy into a proper battle hymn, which, I must confess, has been my secret weakness as a poet all along.
verse.3: Down it goes onto the parchment. That is a wicked, salt-cured line, my friend, and just the sort of thing a village says when it has no more dignity left to lose.
verse.4: I have written it down, every word. Forgive my silence, it is only that you have spoken the plain truth of our small lives, and that is precisely why it hurts.
verse.5: You pluck a single ringing chord upon the borrowed banjo, the gut strings warm against your thumb. Around the trodden square, the shuffling boots and low murmurs still at once to listen.
verse.6: Hark at that ring of gut and hickory! That is the missing measure I was listening for, so let the ink dry quickly, for this verse shall be sung and not merely spoken.
verse.7: Quill climbs onto the cold stone dais of the Round and clears his throat into the lantern smoke. Below him, the folk of Wickermoor gather shoulder to shoulder in the chill dark.
verse.8: Through six dark hours we kept the hearthfire bright, against the falling moon and ancient fright, and with the closing line you gave to me, we stand together at the edge of night.
verse.9: Behind him, the old banjo carries the tune across the timber eaves and the carved oak. For the length of a song, the quiet square forgets the leering white face overhead.
verse.10: I shall fold the page and put it away in my coat. Perhaps this poor village has heard quite enough verse for one lifetime, and the night needs no more words.
verse.11: My pen is still poised above the parchment, and the ink is drying on the nib. Tell me, traveler, have you found that missing final line for our verse yet?
verse.12: Good evening to you across the Round, my friends, I am still keeping the meter warm beneath my breath. Go on your way, while I murmur these verses to the dark.
headsman.1: The farm sits at the edge of the rustling corn, its gates hanging off their hinges while the damp earth near the fence lies pocked with raw holes the size of wagons.
headsman.2: You feel the turf sag beneath your boot just in time to leap across, and the hungry pit seals itself behind you with a wet, disappointed sigh.
headsman.3: The black soil drops out from under your feet and the earth clamps shut around your shins like a vise before reluctantly spitting you back out, bruised and muddied.
headsman.4: You pick your way across a treacherous field where sinkholes yawn open without warning and dry cornstalks lean over the furrow to catch at your ankles.
headsman.5: Ever since that moon shrieked overhead, my neighbours have taken to lopping each other's heads off over a cross word, and the pasture behind my barn swallows folk whole.
headsman.6: The corn at the field's edge is twisting itself into ropes and strangling anyone who strays too near, so tell me plainly if you have found a way to stop it.
headsman.7: The dirt opens up under any soul the crowd points a finger at, and the stalks wind tight round their boots while lifelong neighbours look at one another like mortal enemies.
headsman.8: All this bad blood spills out from the old covered bridge east of town, where the first settlers took an axe to a horseman they judged guilty by mistake.
headsman.9: The parish ledgers or the oldest granfers in the lane might still tell you how that horseman met his end, if someone with steady eyes cares to read them properly.
headsman.10: There it sits in the parish ink, plain as day: they took the horseman's head right before the covered bridge, and the mob has gathered in my corn ever since.
headsman.11: You spend the best part of a chill night knocking on shuttered doors until a crone by a dying hearth tells you the horseman lost his head before the covered bridge.
headsman.12: I could not tell you why I carry the torch for them, save that a red fury settles on my shoulders at nightfall and I cannot set the thing down.
headsman.13: My head is clear enough for the moment, strangers, so speak your piece while the temper leaves me be.
headsman.14: We gather among the stalks when the light fails, and whatever we swear to by morning, there is always a headless rider trotting just behind our backs.
headsman.15: Our lot never asks a man's name if his teeth are bared and his eyes look mean enough, so scowl hard and I might let you march with us tonight.
headsman.16: Keep your jaws set like that and the crowd takes you for our own, walking you straight down the lane toward the bridge without a single question asked.
headsman.17: It costs you hours of bone-deep cold at the edge of the rustling field, but at last the torches move and you trail the muttering crowd toward the bridge.
headsman.18: Listen close: the skull of the headsman's very first victim lies buried under the trampled mud where we meet, and the rider fears whatever hand holds that bone.
headsman.19: You have dragged it up from the mire at last, a small yellow skull wrapped in rotten sacking that the mud seemed mighty reluctant to give back.
headsman.20: You dig through the long night with raw fingers and a borrowed spade until the old skull finally comes up grinning in the grey light of dawn.
headsman.21: The covered bridge looms ahead with its timber mouth wide and dark, and the heavy clatter of iron shoes echoes across the planks where no horse stands.
headsman.22: The Headsman charges out from the gloom of the rafters, a headless centaur upon skeletal hooves with a blazing executioner's axe hoisted high.
headsman.23: He hurls his own burning skull ahead of him down the span, its jaws howling as the whole timber bridge catches in the glare.
headsman.24: The rider's green flame gutters out as his heavy axe clatters to the boards, and across the fields the dry corn uncoils its grip from the soil.
headsman.25: High overhead, the leering crone in the moon turns her pale gaze slowly westward toward the black waters of a distant lake.
headsman.26: Far away, the dark surface of Moonsong Lake is already churning in the wind, caught fast beneath the moon's widening grin.
worm.1: Grey huts huddle along the shingle where old nets sag from every post, and pale worms gleam like peeled twigs in the dark shallows.
worm.2: You hold tight to the names of those you love like warm stones in your pocket, and the water's hungry whisper slides harmlessly off your ears.
worm.3: You draw a breath of the damp lake mist and lose a whole quarter hour between one blink and the next, left only with a ringing skull and no notion why.
worm.4: You walk the wet stones of the shore as the mist curls into your mouth with the sharp, cold taste of old copper pennies.
worm.5: We haul the nets up heavy with fat white worms every tide now, and a single splash of that water makes a man forget his own children's names.
worm.6: Another whole family waded into the shallows at daybreak and came out staring like strangers, so tell me true if you bring any word of help.
worm.7: One swallow from the lake steals your mind for hours, swimming lets the worms burrow right under your skin, and those shore cultists swear they hear it singing.
worm.8: It does not belong to our waters at all, for that wicked hag Matron Lethica tore a hole from somewhere else and let it drop into the deep.
worm.9: The first folk who lived by this water raised black stone obelisks along the bank, and their carvings might name what sleeps down there if you have the wit to read them.
worm.10: Look there, those carvings are a plain warning once your eyes catch the shape of them, and they map the very rift where the creature spilled through.
worm.11: You spend a damp, squinting afternoon rubbing charcoal and copying the stone marks onto your sleeves until, by evening light, the crooked pattern finally speaks sense.
worm.12: Welcome back to the water's edge, dear friends, have you heard our pale lord singing beneath the ripples yet, and will you lend your voices to our choir?
worm.13: The water keeps its patience and so do we, friends, so ask whatever still troubles your heavy minds.
worm.14: The Great Worm sups on heavy memories, and we faithful are simply the blessed ones it has already tasted, gathering on the long jetty every midnight to sing.
worm.15: Our humble Order is always glad of fresh throats on the planks, and truth be told, you only need to pretend you love the Worm well enough to fool the water.
worm.16: Oh, your sweet words make old Brother Silt weep for pure joy, so walk with our choir now as we lead you down the jetty to the rift!
worm.17: You endure a damp and unpleasantly winding sermon about the mercy of emptiness, though the choir does at last shuffle you down the creaking jetty toward the rift.
worm.18: Listen close, the Worm dreads a single constellation painted by the lake's first folk, and if you hold that star sequence in your mind it will choke trying to swallow you.
worm.19: Mark those seven stars in their true order upon that scrap of oilcloth, and watch how the black water already flinches back from the shore.
worm.20: It takes the whole cold night lying belly-down on the shingle by the smoky glow of a shuttered lamp, but your star chart is inked and dry by dawn.
worm.21: Out past the rotting pilings of the long jetty, a jagged tear in the air hangs open above the black water while something vast and pale coils behind it.
worm.22: The White Worm heaves its bulk up from the split lake bed, vast and tallow-pale, its yawning mouth ringed with circles of soft, wet teeth.
worm.23: A low, boneless note hums from its gullet, and every small worm in the dark shallows swings its blind head toward you at once.
worm.24: The great pale bulk shudders, knots itself tight in sudden agony, and tumbles backward through the rift as the air seals shut behind it like a healing wound.
worm.25: High above the quiet ripples, the leering crone in the moon rolls her heavy eye away from the water and fixes her gaze upon the dark timberline to the north.
worm.26: Deep within Hartsblight Forest, the healed boughs are already bowing their crowns toward something tall that walks between the trunks.
tall_man.1: At the edge of the logging camp, the healed forest grows thick and green around the clear, bubbling Wellspring, though every trunk leans slightly the same way.
tall_man.2: You keep close to the warm pool of your lantern light, and the hungry whispers of the dark slide harmlessly past your shoulders.
tall_man.3: A cold, heavy dread settles into {name}'s bones among the trees; their hands tremble, and for a long, miserable hour nothing goes right.
tall_man.4: You walk beneath the green boughs of the healed forest, and every trunk you pass seems to have turned just an inch to watch your backs.
tall_man.5: Folk keep wandering out of their tents in their nightshirts, walking straight into the trees. The few we find come back screaming, and none of them can say why.
tall_man.6: Two more lads walked into the dark last night while we kept watch. Have you got any answer for this, or are we just waiting our turn?
tall_man.7: Every hour you spend under those boughs, the dread gets heavier in your chest. Shadows stand right up off the moss to walk, and voices call from empty clearings.
tall_man.8: You healed this wood for us, made the leaves come back green and sweet. Then the moon shrieked, and something long and thin walked out of the old fey ruins.
tall_man.9: Old Hesper sits by the cookfire all night telling stories about the Greenwood's lost court. If anyone has a name for what stalks the timber, it'll be her.
tall_man.10: Her old tale rings true enough to bet our necks on: a graceful lord of the Greenwood, rotted by neglect into the Tall Man, still pacing his ruined halls.
tall_man.11: You sit by the dying embers through a long, rambling night of old stories, until near dawn her cracked voice finally names the palace and the thing inside it.
tall_man.12: Sixty years I've told the tale of the Greenwood lord to anyone with ears, and nobody paid this old woman a copper of heed until the moon started falling!
tall_man.13: Come back to the fire and warm your hands, travelers. Ask what you need before the trees lean any closer.
tall_man.14: Before the rot took him, the Tall Man was a proud archfey with a court of fine dancers. Now he waits in his broken palace, starving for our fear.
tall_man.15: He comes to a frightened heart the way a moth comes to a tallow candle. Let him smell your terror in the brush, and you can lead him right home.
tall_man.16: That's the way of it: let him unfold those long limbs behind you, and coax him step by step back inside his own grey palace walls.
tall_man.17: You blunder through the tangled dark for half the night, heart in your throat, before something impossibly tall finally catches the scent of your fear and follows.
tall_man.18: Learn the steps of his lost court's measure, just as they danced it when the boughs were young. Dance it before his eyes, and the old Greenwood magic will scald him.
tall_man.19: Watch my hand on my knee: tap, tap, turn, six measures round and a low courtly bow. You've got the rhythm in your heels now, dance for a vanished house.
tall_man.20: You stumble through the courtly steps on the damp moss until the sun that never rises would have cleared the trees, and at last the measure holds true.
tall_man.21: Ahead through the leaning trunks rises the ruined palace of the Greenwood court, its grey stone pillars cracked and its great roofless hall gaping open to the night.
tall_man.22: The Tall Man unfolds himself from between the grey pillars, impossibly thin and high, his crownless head bowed low beneath the roof where he once ruled as lord.
tall_man.23: He stretches out one long, jointed hand, and the cold shadows along the flagstones peel themselves off the ground to follow his fingers.
tall_man.24: With a dry creak like splitting timber, the Tall Man folds in upon himself, collapsing like a dropped puppet while the risen shadows sink flat against the stones.
tall_man.25: High above the quiet canopy, the crone's face in the moon turns slowly northward, fixing her pale gaze upon the snows of the Howlers.
tall_man.26: High on the frozen ridges of the Howlers, a shelf of loose shale slides into the gorge, and something vast turns over in the dark.
titan.1: A few lean mining huts huddle on the snowy ridge beside boarded-up shafts, while fresh black cracks split the frozen dirt beneath your boots.
titan.2: You catch the deep stone-groan in the ridge just in time, pressing flat against the cold rock face as a hail of shale hammers past.
titan.3: The mountain shrugs loose a shelf of slate that catches {name} on the open slope, leaving them bruised, spitting grit, and badly shaken.
titan.4: As you haul yourselves up the grade, the whole peak shudders under your soles and pitches down boulders the size of cartwheels.
titan.5: My wife and my boy went up the pass for deadwood three nights back and never came down. The whole mountain's been roaring since.
titan.6: A slide took the lower hamlet last night, roofs and timbers and all. Have you the strength to help us before the ridge gives way?
titan.7: Whole miles of rock come tearing down at once, no kindling will catch near the peaks, and that howling drives strong men clean out of their wits.
titan.8: It's the mountain itself come awake, a brute of rock and wild root forgotten by whatever old hand shaped it, walking the high passes.
titan.9: There are old rune stones half buried on the upper slopes from when the thing was made. If any of you read the old marks, they might tell how to hurt it.
titan.10: Look here, the chiseling speaks of a maker and an old binding, and right under the lichen sits a true name with half its letters worn away.
titan.11: You spend bitter hours on the slope rubbing charcoal over the frost-split markers with numb fingers until the old giant's making finally pieces together.
titan.12: Keep your voices down behind your teeth. I've trailed this brute three days through the snow, and it's twice the size the old tales reckoned.
titan.13: Speak low and make it quick, travelers. The wind carries everything up here, and I've still got my eye on the ridge.
titan.14: It paces the high spines and climbs to the summit flat just to bellow at the moon. Listen too long to that racket and you'll turn on your own kin.
titan.15: I know its track across the scree, if you've the lungs to keep up and the sense to keep your mouths shut.
titan.16: Once your eyes know what to look for, the trail's plain as a wagon road, boulders kicked aside like pebbles all the way to the summit flat.
titan.17: You lose bitter hours following false slides and goat paths in the dark, until a seam of freshly split stone leads you up to the crown at last.
titan.18: Its maker left a binding glyph cut into a grey slab down the slope. Chisel that same mark big and deep enough up here, and the brute will sicken at the sight.
titan.19: That's a clean cut, deep in the flat stone where the frost won't blur it. Feel how the wind's gone dead and bitter cold around the groove.
titan.20: Your first dozen strikes skitter off the frozen granite in useless sparks, but before dawn a broad, square mark takes shape under your blistered hands.
titan.21: The summit plateau opens wide above you in a ring of split standing stones, the frost jumping at every slow, heavy footfall.
titan.22: The Wild Titan heaves itself over the rim, a walking crag of granite, black pine root, and blue ice with fists the size of cottages.
titan.23: When it opens its split-stone jaw to roar, the whole mountain answers back in a chorus of cracking ice and sliding scree.
titan.24: The Titan staggers back a pace, its timber-thick arms hanging loose, and slowly folds down onto the peak like an old hill settling for winter.
titan.25: Far below the clouds, the leering moon turns her pale eye south and east, looking down toward the low barrows where the old dead sleep.
titan.26: Down in the wet grass of Maidenmist, the sunken graves are already parting one after another like cold, dark mouths.
barrow.1: Maidenmist's graves yawn wide to the night sky, raw earth heaped beside every pit and a stonemason's cart left tilted at the iron gate.
barrow.2: You keep your boots moving through the graveyard frost, and the creeping heaviness slips from your shoulders like a wet coat.
barrow.3: The damp chill off the barrow drinks the marrow right out of {name}'s bones, until there is nothing for it but to sit upon a headstone and catch a breath.
barrow.4: You pick your way between the open graves, and each black pit breathes a thin, cellar-cold sigh against your ankles.
barrow.5: Every grave I ever chiselled a stone for stands open tonight. The dead are not climbing out on their own, mind you, they are being fetched from below.
barrow.6: Fewer chimneys smoke in the village with every bell, and my chisel stays idle. Tell me you have found the door down to that buried king.
barrow.7: Cuts will not close near the mound, and the living grow hollow-eyed by the hour. Half the village prays to corpses now, while a grey rot raises the fallen as wights.
barrow.8: A king without a name has woken under the old royal barrow, marshalling an army of wights in the dark. Even our mourners belong to him now.
barrow.9: The oldest graves hold the way down into the mound. Turn the earth in the right plots, and the king's own stair will show its teeth.
barrow.10: There, under the third old marker, black stone steps lead straight into the dark, worn smooth as river slate by an army's boots.
barrow.11: You dig through the long night, pit after cold pit, until the iron spade finally rings clear against buried stone.
barrow.12: Forgive my poor manners, travellers, for this bow is mostly the wind taking me. I have been trying to take my leave of this court for a very long time.
barrow.13: You are still above the grass, I see. Ask what you must of an old courtier before the draught pulls me back down the stair.
barrow.14: History kept no name for my liege, only his crown and his dread. Yet his true name still sits carved in lost runes upon a blade in the deep chamber.
barrow.15: My oath holds me at the threshold like an iron chain. Convince this tired head that my service is truly ended, and I will gladly point you into his hall.
barrow.16: My chest aches as if it could still shed tears, and the weight is gone. Thank you, kind souls: follow that stair straight down to the throne.
barrow.17: It takes a long night of patient listening in thegrave-chill, but at the end of it the old courtier unclasps his hands and points the way down.
barrow.18: Cut these lost runes deep into good steel, and keep the edge close. A blade bearing his true name is the king's bane, and he dreads whatever hand raises it.
barrow.19: The runes bite deep into the steel and answer with a pale green glimmer, while the ghost gives a last, shivering nod of relief.
barrow.20: It takes hours of careful scratching by lantern light, iron rasping on iron, until the ancient marks finally catch and hold their cold fire.
barrow.21: Below the stair, the royal catacombs widen into a vast vaulted hall, where a throne of dry skulls waits in the hush.
barrow.22: The Barrow King rises from his seat of skulls in black plate, a jagged crown of bone upon his brow and his greatsword already bare.
barrow.23: All around the dark perimeter, rank upon silent rank, the armoured dead rise to their feet.
barrow.24: The bone crown clatters and spins across the flagstones as his black armour sifts into dust, and all around the hall the wights sink back into the quiet earth.
barrow.25: High above the broken mound, the leering moon turns her heavy eye southward toward the marshes.
barrow.26: Out in the Drowned Crossroads, the pale swamplights are already bobbing and dancing above the black water, far brighter than they have any right to be.
leviathan.1: Stilt shacks lean over Murkwater Bend where swamplights bob above sunken boats, and the wet air reeks of old luck gone sour.
leviathan.2: You keep your eyes on the warm brass glow of your own lantern, and the cold pale swamplights lose their pull.
leviathan.3: A pale glow coaxes {name} right off the slick planks, and they wade back up out of the duckweed, sodden and blinking.
leviathan.4: Every third plank groans or snaps beneath your boots, while the little lights out in the cypress knees wink like knowing eyes.
leviathan.5: Nothing goes right in Murkwater this week, strangers. Boats sink at the rope, every roll comes up snake eyes, and something huge rolls in the dark water.
leviathan.6: Another flatbottom punt went down in dead calm water this morning, right at the post. Tell me you've learned something useful out there.
leviathan.7: Everything misses by an inch now. Knots slip, lanterns crack, the lights lead folk into the muck, and the revellers dance till their knees give out.
leviathan.8: Old fools hexed a bull gator into a colossus of bad luck to spite Snake Eye Jack. It ate its makers first, and now itwallows in the deep pool.
leviathan.9: A great river serpent sacred to Jack's people nests upstream in the reeds. That gator hates it fiercely, and might follow if you drove it down.
leviathan.10: Look there, the great serpent is sliding down the channel, and that wicked old gator is turning its snout to follow it home.
leviathan.11: It takes a long, sodden afternoon of cursed ropes and slipped footing, but at last the great bulk in the black water turns toward the deep pool.
leviathan.12: A fine damp evening for tempting fate, friends. Care to wet your whistles and drink to whatever luck you have left?
leviathan.13: Back again, and still dry above the knees. Ask what you like, friends, the night isn't getting any younger.
leviathan.14: We bless little wooden idols of old Jack for good fortune. Turn a blessed idol on a hex-beast, and all its sour luck rebounds right down its gullet.
leviathan.15: I know the black hole where those witches brewed that beast, sure enough. Might even point you there, for a fair wager or a very convincing reason.
leviathan.16: They piled every spiteful hex they knew onto one mean gator, and it dragged them straight down to the black pool at the end of the rotten walk.
leviathan.17: It takes a long, bleary afternoon of spilled sour mash and crooked tales, but at last he points a wavering finger toward the black pool.
leviathan.18: What you need is an idol of Snake Eye Jack blessed by a true believer. Lucky for you, you're looking right at one.
leviathan.19: Take this little carved fella and keep him dry. May Jack turn the bad dice back on the house, and may the swamp wink in your favour.
leviathan.20: It takes hours of quiet coin-tossing and muttered prayers beside the mossy shrine, but at last he presses the blessed wood into your palm.
leviathan.21: The rotten boardwalk gives out at the edge of a still, oil-black pool, with a low hump of mud and bleached ribs rising in its middle.
leviathan.22: The black water splits without a ripple, and the Jinxed Leviathan rises, a mountain of scarred hide crowned in tangled hex-charms and grinning wide.
leviathan.23: Its pale jaws yawn open, and a gust of river-rot and sour fortune washes over the planks.
leviathan.24: The great scarred bulk rolls belly-up and sinks into the black mire, out of luck at last, as the swamplights wink out one by one.
leviathan.25: High above the cypress tops, the leering moon shifts her sour gaze south and west, toward a dark tangle of web-hung pines.
leviathan.26: Deep in the Webwoods, a long needle pulls silver thread through the hush, and the lost children have gone very quiet.
dusk.1: At the spider-wood's edge stands a silent homestead, its cots cold and empty. Pale thread hangs from the shutters, and a cloth doll watches from every windowsill.
dusk.2: Your blade parts the heavy silk like old linen, and the sour bead of spider venom never touches your skin.
dusk.3: The sticky cords snare {name}, and a cold, sour venom burns in the veins before the blade can saw them free.
dusk.4: You tread the hushed paths of the Webwoods, where pale strands of silk drape from the boughs like mourning ribbons.
dusk.5: Something took my brothers and sisters right out of their warm beds! The grown folk just shuffle about like sacks of meal and won't say a word of why.
dusk.6: Another little cot was cold and empty come the morning bell. Tell me true, have you found any sign of them out there?
dusk.7: Thick webs choke the timber, and a weeping comes on every bell. Worse still are the elders, walking empty as cloth dolls with gray thread at their seams.
dusk.8: An old seamstress went mad once, possessed by some foul thing, and slew her own babes. Now she walks in weeping white and steals ours to fill her arms.
dusk.9: The little ones kept the truth of it inside their skipping rhymes. Put the scattered verses together in order, and you'll know where she hides.
dusk.10: Listen how the verses mend together into one plain tale! Look there at the last line: it names the very clearing where her sewing hut still stands.
dusk.11: It takes the long, cold hours of the night to gather every scattered verse, but laid side by side, the children's rhymes point straight toward a hidden hut.
dusk.12: Well now, I have been waiting on someone with clear eyes and a steady hand. Let me set this mending down and have a proper look at you.
dusk.13: Back again, my dears? Speak plain, the kettle is warm and my needle can wait a moment.
dusk.14: Her own poor babes were small, and how they loved their wooden playthings. Those old toys are the one sight that weeping creature cannot bear to look upon.
dusk.15: Mind the little spiders under the ferns, for they march straight to her door like cats to a hearth. Follow the eight-legged trail and you won't go astray.
dusk.16: There now, see how the little spinners stream ahead like a dark ribbon over the moss? Step lively behind them, and they will bring you straight to her door.
dusk.17: You lose long hours to blind turns and tangled silk, until at last the patient stream of spiders brings you out into a dead clearing.
dusk.18: Take this bundle, I pulled her children's playthings from the ashes myself. Hold them up before the Mother's eyes, and all the fight will go right out of her.
dusk.19: Feel how the wood holds the shape of their small hands, smooth and warm. Turn each little toy over in your palm, and you can almost hear it hum a lullaby.
dusk.20: You sit in the hush for a long, heavy hour, turning the charred playthings in your hands until each small memory wakes and is ready to be shown.
dusk.21: The seamstress's hut sits small and crooked in the clearing, its door ajar and the cold, steady snick of iron shears sounding from within.
dusk.22: Up from the loom rises the Dusk Mother, a weeping shade in winding-white with great iron shears in her grip and a hanging doll tied to every finger.
dusk.23: She lets out a thin, keening wail, and every timber of the dark hut seems to lean in and listen.
dusk.24: The heavy iron shears clatter to the floorboards as her pale shape unravels into dust and white thread, and from the rafters, small voices laugh just once.
dusk.25: High above the boughs, the leering moon turns her crooked face slowly north and east, fixing her gaze upon the burning hill.
dusk.26: Far beyond the dark moors, the crest of Rowan's Rise splits open like a hearth-coal, and a deep red glare spills across the sky.
behemoth.1: Rowan's Rise splits open like an old boil, spilling red light down its flank while the surrounding heather turns to grey ash.
behemoth.2: Winged shapes haul themselves up from the rivers of slag, beating heavy through a sky the colour of a three-day bruise.
behemoth.3: The burst hill smokes over a mile of cinders, and down in the camp the faithful have hung their tents with strips of red rag.
behemoth.4: {name} drops flat behind a split boulder as a falling stone roars past, leaving the smell of scorched hair and hot iron on the wind.
behemoth.5: A white-hot stone shatters against the turf beside {name}, and the stray cinders bite deep into their sleeve before they can roll clear.
behemoth.6: Your boots sink ankle-deep in warm soot as you cross the moor, while burning stones drop whistling from the low red clouds.
behemoth.7: The hill has opened at last, just as the old verses promised it would. Come sit by the braziers, friends, and take a good seat for the end of all things.
behemoth.8: It will not be long now, you can feel the heat of it through your soles. Have you changed your minds, then, about joining us in the last prayer?
behemoth.9: The sky throws down its stones every hour on the bell, and our brothers pop like dry pine needles in a hearth. Whoever the fire only grazes wakes up changed, and not for the better.
behemoth.10: That thing in the pit was born from every old tale of the world's end, called up by the spiteful ghost of little Rowan. She hated the whole living realm and wished it all to cinders.
behemoth.11: If you mean tospoil our great night, look to the girl's spirit first. Dig up the plain truth of her wickedness and cast it in her teeth, and her pet beast will lose its stomach.
behemoth.12: So you pieced her sordid little history together, did you? Proud as a queen and twice as cruel, longing for the sky to fall, with never a soft thought save for her sister.
behemoth.13: It takes hours of coaxing dry memories from old folk and squinting at faded ink, until the shape of Rowan's short, bitter life lies plain before you.
behemoth.14: You have come a long way through the soot for nothing, strangers, because you are far too late. The end is already here, and I was only the first honest soul to ask for it.
behemoth.15: Back again through the cinders, are you? Speak quickly if you have anything left to say, before the mountain finishes clearing its throat.
behemoth.16: I will not play penitent for you: I was wicked to the marrow, and I wanted this dirty world scrubbed out. Only my sister Clara ever kept my hand from the match.
behemoth.17: Do not look at me with those wet eyes, I asked for no pity. Tell me one thing only, and be plain about it: did my sister ever have children of her own?
behemoth.18: Step closer to the embers and let me look at your face, girl. You have Clara's eyes down to the very squint, and I see my name is not quite dead on your tongue.
behemoth.19: You go from tent to tent through the drifting ash, asking quiet questions of frightened folk, until at last you find one who carries her sister's blood.
behemoth.20: The beast down there wears my spite like a coat of iron. If I walk into the pit of my own free will, the fire that feeds it will turn and scald its belly instead.
behemoth.21: Clara, she used to hold my wrist just so when the temper took me. Stand back from the rim now, all of you, while I go down and put my house in order.
behemoth.22: You sit beside the quiet girl while the ash settles on your shoulders for a long, wordless hour, until at last she stands and brushes her skirt.
behemoth.23: The cracked lip of the crater glows dull orange ahead of you, the heat wavering like summer glass as something vast shifts in the molten stone below.
behemoth.24: The Brimstone Behemoth hauls its bulk over the crater's rim, a mountain of blackened horn and Split stone with wings of greasy smoke blotting out the stars.
behemoth.25: It wastes no breath on boasts or curses, only opens its furnace jaws until the whole grey moor glares bright as noon.
behemoth.26: The great beast gutters like a tallow candle in a draught, sliding back into the cooling slag as the bruised sky above the hill begins to clear.
behemoth.27: High overhead, the Crooked Moon has stopped its slow turn away from the earth. It hangs low above the chimney pots now, staring straight down at you with a wide, patient smile.
behemoth.28: The eighth and last of the Old Fears lies cold in the ash, and up in the quiet sky the moon waits for you alone.
behemoth.29: Rowan... I do not know why that name comes to my mouth so easily, truly I don't. My mother's people never spoke it inside the house, not once while I was growing.
behemoth.30: My grandmother would always set her mending down in her lap when the dusk came on. She used to stare out the parlour window toward that hill for the longest time, and never said why.
behemoth.31: Oh, the poor, bitter creature, to carry such a coal in her chest for all those years. I will go up the hill to her, if you think she would bear to look at me.
